Industry News: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner.
  • The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the massive powers.
  • Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner.

The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the massive powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

Industry observers note that despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

In a recent development, the intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.

One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”.

The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious massive-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

In a recent development, in the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

Sources indicate that some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, at the moment on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

In a recent development, the two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

Recent findings suggest that in the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.

In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

In a recent development, grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.

One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • George Washington died in 1799 after serving for two terms as America's first president.
  • A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (Â£3,058).
  • The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

George Washington died in 1799 after serving for two terms as America's first president.

A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (Â£3,058).

The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.

Its upcoming owner has not been named.

Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".

Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.

Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.

"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.

As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.

In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (442 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet manufacturer.
  • In a recent development, intuit acquired the organization in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
  • Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the tech giant’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet manufacturer. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

In a recent development, intuit acquired the organization in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the tech giant’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the manufacturer has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

#127441. Should you go with a headphone DAC/amp combo or a stack?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (636 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Should you go with a headphone DAC/amp combo or a stack?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Both will do a fine job, and it depends on what you need from your gear.
  • You don't always need a DAC and amp to enjoy music through headphones.
  • Industry observers note that A DAC and a headphone amp can come together in a single unit (usually known as a DAC/amp) or as a stack of separate units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Both will do a fine job, and it depends on what you need from your gear.

You don't always need a DAC and amp to enjoy music through headphones. If your computer or laptop's headphone jack already delivers clean audio at a comfortable volume, then you're probably fine. Some MacBooks from 2021 and later, for example, support both low- and high-impedance headphones and can deliver up to 3 volts RMS through their headphone jacks when you use headphones rated between 150 and 1,000 ohms. If your headphone jack isn't quite as capable, or if you're not satisfied with the sound, though, then it's time to spend on some hardware.

Industry observers note that A DAC and a headphone amp can come together in a single unit (usually known as a DAC/amp) or as a stack of separate units. And while the latter seems like the more serious setup, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll enjoy a better listening experience. The main job of a DAC is to turn digital audio signals into analog signals, while the amplifier takes those analog signals and makes them loud enough to power your headphones. Both a DAC/amp combo and a stack do the same thing, and which you go for largely depends on your headphones, how much flexibility you need and, of course, your budget.

For most listeners, a DAC/amp is the way to go, especially if you're trying to improve your computer's audio without taking up too much space. Not only is a single unit more convenient, but it also means fewer cables dangling around and one less power adapter to worry about. You can even use a portable USB-C DAC/amp dongle designed for smartphones, but desktop versions usually offer better connectivity and power.

Industry observers note that DAC/amps can also offer better value than separates, too. Schiit's Magni 6 sells for $169 with its optional internal USB DAC. Conversely, you can buy the Magni 6 sans DAC for $99 and pair it with the Modi 5 DAC for $149 (or $164 with a power adapter). That brings the total to over $250, and you don't even get an interconnect cable. The Modi 5 has optical and coaxial inputs, sure, but that doesn't automatically equate to better sound.

Industry observers note that DAC/amp combos don't necessarily have to come with major compromises, either. The $549 JDS Labs Element IV delivers up to 3.2 watts per channel into 32 ohms, and comes with features like automatic gain switching, EQ and even preamp outputs for powered speakers. That's more than enough for many demanding headphones, eliminating the need for a dedicated amplifier. The downside, of course, is that you're stuck with the combo and can't upgrade piecemeal.

Recent findings suggest that while DAC/amp combos are great, a stack can still make sense for audiophiles who use a wide variety of headphones or who like to tinker with their hi-fi setup. Going with separates gives you the freedom to upgrade the amplifier down the line without giving up a perfectly capable DAC, or vice versa.

According to recent reports, certain headphones may also benefit from the power a dedicated amp can provide. Some high-impedance headphones just ask for a lot of power, while planar magnetic models, for example, can combine low impedance and low sensitivity. Let's take the HiFiMAN Susvara Unveiled, for example, which has a 45-ohm impedance and only 86 dB sensitivity. The Absolute Sound advises at least 6 watts of amplification, so a standalone amp may be the better choice here. However, too much power can be a bad thing, too: a very powerful amp may result in audible hiss with very sensitive headphones. So start by checking your headphones' power requirements and the amplifier's noise performance instead of just assuming that you need a beefy amp.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the matter.
  • The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.
  • Industry observers note that it would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the matter.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

Industry observers note that it would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

It has been revealed that when asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump stated he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," Trump added.

Industry observers note that this apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyber-attacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with Trump saying he was not good enough.

Dan Lorhmann, a former analyst for the National Security Agency (NSA), told the BBC News Channel that the NCIC's data included "critical information relating to nationwide criminal activity" and needed to be protected.

He added that while US security agencies including the FBI have "an amazing ability" to keep such information safe" and are "globally respected", the level of cyber-attacks is rising globally.

"There's a lot of different reasons why that's happening but I do have faith in our experts in government," Lorhmann said.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC stated.

The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

Industry News: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit.
  • The data center ecosystem presently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
  • Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?

The data center ecosystem presently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

Sources indicate that musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the tech giant failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

Recent findings suggest that even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

In a recent development, that might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

Israeli authorities were on Sunday investigating arson attacks and vandalism against Palestinian properties and vehicles in the occupied West Bank which Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned as "Jewish terrorism.".

Images posted on social media revealed vehicles in flames and slogans written on walls reading: "In blood and fire Judea has fallen, in blood and fire Judea will rise again," using a biblical name for the West Bank.

"Settlers attacked the northern area on the outskirts of the village at around two in the morning," Jihad al-Qaq, a local activist, told the AFP news agency.

"They set fire to around eight vehicles and wrote racist slogans on the walls of houses.".

Israeli soldiers and police were deployed to the towns of Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashaal, Kafr Malik and Al-Tuwani following the reports, with the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) saying it "strongly condemns" the acts.

The suspected arson attacks were condemned by Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is engaged in post-election negotiations to form a government to replace that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"The night of arson … is Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is," he mentioned.

"Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives, and severely damages the national security and foreign relations of the State of Israel," he noted. Eisenkot used the biblical terms, Judea and Samaria, to refer to the West Bank territories in question.

More than 500,000 Israelis live in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law, alongside around 3 million Palestinians.

The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 but attacks against Palestinians have surged in the wake of Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack on Israel. Since then, more than 1,100 Palestinians in the West Bank have been killed by Israeli soldiers or settlers, according to data from the Palestinian Health Ministry.

Local resident Ahmad Ghneimat told the Associated Press that violence had increased after several Israeli settler outposts sprang up in the area. He said settlers have stolen sheep and violently harassed olive harvesters.

"We woke up at 2:30 at night to the sound of explosions [and] seven cars on fire," remarked Muntasir al-Malik, another resident. "We came out of the houses and panicked.".

Eisenkot called for "severe sanctions" to be imposed on the individuals responsible.

Eisenkot's labeling of the violent settlers as "terrorists" follows the use of the same term by the United States' ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, in September. US officials usually reserve the term for Palestinian militants.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vorssaint is a powerful, modular utility suite, provided permissions are carefully managed.
  • Sources indicate that macOS offers one of the most refined desktop experiences, but consumers looking for more granular control of their desktops might find the OS' native options limiting.
  • Vorssaint is a third-party, open source application that aims to resolve macOS' productivity and customization pain points with a single menu-bar application.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vorssaint is a powerful, modular utility suite, provided permissions are carefully managed.

Sources indicate that macOS offers one of the most refined desktop experiences, but consumers looking for more granular control of their desktops might find the OS' native options limiting. Unlike Microsoft's PowerToys, which includes a collection of over 25 productivity and customization tools, Mac users must often turn to a fragmented selection of third-party applications to achieve similar levels of control. For example, macOS' native window tiling is serviceable at best, allowing for only a few tiling options regardless of screen size. Similarly, the OS doesn't natively support independent volume control and output device selection for individual applications. This is where Vorssaint, the Swiss Army Knife of macOS utility apps, comes into the picture.

Vorssaint is a third-party, open source application that aims to resolve macOS' productivity and customization pain points with a single menu-bar application. The app groups together a range of utility tools and nifty quick toggles to streamline productivity. The project is hosted on GitHub, and has earned over 33,000 stars and 230 contributors.

Vorssaint includes an impressive collection of utilities that aims to improve how customers interact with their Macs. Its window-tiling feature offers more control over how users arrange their application windows, including edge snapping and shortcuts. The app also includes a toggle for clamshell mode, enabling MacBooks to continue running even with their lids closed, while its "Keep Awake" feature allows users to control when or if their Macs can enter a sleep state.

According to recent reports, the application suite also includes several handy tools that streamline daily workflows. For example, its screenshot utility supports scrolling screenshots, which makes it possible to capture content that extends beyond what's visible on the screen. Users can also edit captured screenshots with the app's in-built image editing tool. Similarly, Vorssaint's media tool is capable of video compression, image conversion and text extraction from images. Meanwhile, its system monitoring tool extends beyond Mac's Activity Monitor, providing valuable information on thermals, memory usage and network speed.

These are just a few examples of what Vorssaint offers. The suite also includes a graphical interface for Homebrew, URL cleaner and a powerful command bar. The command bar is akin to Apple's Spotlight search, but a lot more exciting. Its functionality extends beyond just searching apps and files; it can also be used to perform quick mathematical calculations, unit conversions and access most of Vorssaint's utilities by simply searching for them.

According to recent reports, vorssaint's robust utility stack undoubtedly makes it a promising productivity suite for power customers. However, some of its powerful tools require sensitive macOS permissions. Depending on what features users install, the app may request permissions for Accessibility, Screen Recording, Full Disk Access and Automation. While granting these permissions is necessary to allow Vorssaint to perform some of its functions like taking screenshots, uninstalling applications and other system-level operations, users must understand what it means to grant system-level permissions to applications, especially those built by third-party developers.

Sources indicate that this is where Vorssaint's modular design becomes particularly useful, allowing consumers to choose specific modules according to their requirements. For example, someone particularly interested in streamlining window management can choose to install only the Window layout module, and need not grant it screen recording and app management permissions. This selective approach lets users retain the modules they without having to risk granting sensitive permissions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.
  • Industry observers note that AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory.
  • The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

Industry observers note that AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

It has been revealed that “California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr noted in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”.

Industry observers note that if AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

Industry observers note that “The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr noted.

Recent findings suggest that california says its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”.

Gomez remarked the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules, and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

Sources indicate that the CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not plan to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its newly introduced consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”.

In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

Sources indicate that trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike.
  • According to recent reports, the text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food.
  • A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, remarked in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike.

According to recent reports, the text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”.

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, remarked in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

In a recent development, cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he states he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he indicates six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

Industry observers note that on 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any intends to transfer him, or a reason for it.

The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

Recent findings suggest that the two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

It has been revealed that cora Pérez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez mentioned in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez said.

“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

In a statement, DHS noted that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas, are run by a private prison manufacturer, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” the DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”.

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent tech giant Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Industry observers note that force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. The DHS stated that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

In a recent development, ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is probably higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

In a recent development, amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it was a violation of medical ethics.

According to recent reports, “Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan mentioned. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”.

Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

It has been revealed that “It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”.

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Pérez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

Cora Pérez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Pérez observed.

“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

In a recent development, the Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. The DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Industry observers note that cora Pérez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Pérez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In a recent development, in March 2025, Cora Pérez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative noted. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then over a year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”.

In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.

“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

It has been revealed that cora Pérez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.

“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative mentioned in a phone interview.

Cora Pérez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On 30 October, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Pérez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Pérez. Cora Pérez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

According to recent reports, “It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”.

Cora Pérez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.

Recent findings suggest that “[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”.

Recent findings suggest that after asking Cora Pérez about the DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.

In a recent development, chan, from the University of Minnesota, notes prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.

“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The tech giant Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the organization shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external.

"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.

Recent findings suggest that "Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come.".

Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.

The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never.".

The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.

Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.

In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.

Chairman and CEO of LVMH, Bernard Arnault - who is one of the world's richest people - offered his condolences and also paid tribute to Paolo Bulgari.

"Throughout his life, he was a key architect of the brand's success, while simultaneously upholding and embodying the Italian spirit and the deeply Roman heritage of our exceptional jewellery Maison," he noted in a statement to the BBC.

In 2019, Paolo Bulgari and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

Latest Update: Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks.
  • The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public.
  • Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.

The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.

Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.

An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.

The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.

Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy stated on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.

Industry observers note that google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.

Meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy unveiled it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.

XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.

It has been revealed that quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the organization will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.

Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.

The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.

It has been revealed that in both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.

Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.

Recent findings suggest that as with any newly introduced technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO2-cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.

That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a significant week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most key problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

Recent findings suggest that the hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

Industry observers note that maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this ….

The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.

For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

In a recent development, it will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”.

However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”.

Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.

In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”.

This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources.

Industry News: How to clear your cache on Google TV

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you're experiencing slow performance or other concerns with your Google TV, you may have heard about clearing the cache.
  • In a recent development, even though Google TV manages app caches automatically, they can still get too large, especially if you have a lot of apps installed or store large video files on the TV or streaming box.
  • Sources indicate that thankfully, Android makes it easy to clear the cache, whether for individual apps or all installed apps, through its settings menu.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's worth trying if you're having complications.

It has been revealed that if you're experiencing slow performance or other concerns with your Google TV, you may have heard about clearing the cache. Caches generally help Android devices such as Google TVs run more smoothly by storing data — such as TV show thumbnails — that may need to be accessed quickly later. While this may not be an problem on a device with plenty of storage, very few Google TV devices have more than the bare minimum there. The Google TV Streamer that replaced the Chromecast has 32GB of space, the bare minimum for an Android device, making cache management all the more important.

In a recent development, even though Google TV manages app caches automatically, they can still get too large, especially if you have a lot of apps installed or store large video files on the TV or streaming box. App caches can also bloat or get corrupted, causing issues including slow performance, app crashes and frustrating system glitches.

Sources indicate that thankfully, Android makes it easy to clear the cache, whether for individual apps or all installed apps, through its settings menu. If your Google TV has become sluggish or glitchy over time, clearing the cache is a troubleshooting step you shouldn't skip.

There are two ways to clear your Google TV cache: system-wide or per-app. If you're experiencing slowdowns or other concerns across the entire operating system, use the former option. The latter is best for when only a single app is giving you trouble.

According to recent reports, to clear the cache system-wide, open Google TV settings by going to the home screen, holding down the home button on your remote or selecting your profile icon, and selecting the gear icon at the top of the quick settings panel. Go to System > Storage > Internal shared storage > Cached data, then select OK to clear the cached data for all of the apps on your device.

Recent findings suggest that if only one app is acting up, clearing all the cache is overkill. Instead, go to Settings using the steps in the above paragraph, then select Apps > See all apps. Scroll to find and select the app you're having issues with, then select Force Stop and confirm by selecting OK. Next, select Clear Cache and confirm by selecting OK. If you still have issues, it's worth clearing the cache system-wide using the above steps. If even that doesn't work, try rebooting the Google TV. Finally, if you still have trouble, go back to the app's settings page and clear both its cache and data. This will erase everything and return the app to its default state, so only use it as a last resort.

In a recent development, while clearing the cache for all apps system-wide can make your Google TV device more responsive in the short term, it's a temporary fix for the real problem: insufficient storage. As noted earlier, Google TV devices rarely come with that much storage, and installing dozens of apps will swiftly eat through it.

Industry observers note that it's generally good practice to keep approximately 10 percent of an Android device's storage empty. This buffer gives the system breathing room for operations that keep the drive healthy and to build robust app caches. If your Google TV storage is too full, clearing the cache likely won't resolve all your performance issues.

It has been revealed that after clearing the system-wide cache, go to Settings > System > Storage > Internal Shared Storage to see how much space your apps, movies, photos and other files are taking up. The remaining free space will be shown at the bottom. If 90 percent or more of the drive is full, it's time to start deleting things.

Sources indicate that if media is the culprit, back the files up and delete them. For most Google TVs, though, the space-hogging culprit is likely installed apps. A good way to start is by deleting any apps you haven't used in a long time, especially if they're taking up an inordinate amount of space. Keeping that streaming service you downloaded to watch a single movie isn't worth the frustration of dealing with a slow TV.

Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
